title: Ch.5: FIRST LANGUAGE ACQUISITION & BILINGUAL FIRST LANGUAGE (2L1)
content:
Chapter 5: First Language Acquisition & Two First Languages # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 5. Link to Chapter 5
1. Pre-Class Overview & Core Orientation # 1.1 Chapter Focus # This chapter explores the developmental trajectory of monolingual first language (L1) acquisition (sound, vocabulary, grammar, semantics/pragmatics) and bilingual first language (2L1) acquisition, with a focus on how children build linguistic systems from infancy to early childhood.
1.2 Key Learning Objectives # By the end of this chapter, learners will be able to:
Explain the stages and mechanisms of L1 sound system acquisition (perception, segmentation, production). Identify the cognitive assumptions that solve the “Gavagai Problem” in vocabulary learning. Describe the development of functional morphology (e.g., past tense) and syntax (e.g., wh-questions) in L1. Analyze why semantic (aspect) and pragmatic (scalar implicatures) acquisition are delayed relative to other linguistic domains. Distinguish between “one system” vs. “two systems” in 2L1 acquisition and recognize cross-linguistic influence. 1.3 Guiding Questions for Reading # How do infants transition from universal sound sensitivity to native phoneme categorization? Why are verbs harder to learn than nouns in L1 vocabulary development? What evidence supports the “two separate grammars” claim in bilingual first language acquisition? How do computational complexity and cognitive maturity affect semantic/pragmatic learning? 2. Core Content Modules (By Section) # Each section follows a “Core Content (Key Concepts + Study Examples) → In-Class Activity” structure, aligned with instructor teaching notes.
2.1 Section 5.1: Acquisition of the Sounds of One’s Native Language # Focuses on how children “break into” the speech signal by mastering three components of the sound system:
1. Segmental Inventory: From Universal Sensitivity to Native Categorization # Key Problem: Children must identify 40–50 native phonemes from 800+ global phonetic units (the “phoneme categorization problem”). Developmental Stages: 6–8 Months: Universal Perceptual Sensitivity
Infants detect all linguistically relevant sound contrasts (not just native ones). Example 1 (Eimas et al. 1971): 1–4 month-olds dishabituate to English /b/ vs. /p/ (e.g., bin vs. pin), proving they distinguish non-produced contrasts. Example 2 (Werker & Tees 1984): 6–8 month-olds (English/Hindi-learning) distinguish Hindi dental [d] vs. retroflex [d]; by 10–12 months, only Hindi learners retain this sensitivity. 10–12 Months+: Native Phoneme Categorization
Infants “prune” universal sensitivity to focus on native phonemes (e.g., English infants retain [l]/[r] distinction; Japanese infants lose it, as Japanese merges [l]/[r] into one phoneme). 2. Segmentation Problem: Finding Word Boundaries # Key Challenge: Speech has no “silent spaces” (unlike writing); children use three language-specific cues: Cue 1: Isolated Words: Caretaker speech (6–60 isolated words/hour) acts as “anchors” (e.g., knowing Daddy helps segment Daddy knows into Daddy + knows). Cue 2: Prosody (Stress): The “Prosodic Bootstrapping Hypothesis”—English uses trochaic stress (first syllable stressed: BA-by, SPON-sor), so children assume stressed syllables mark word starts (90% accurate for English). Cue 3: Phonotactics: Language-specific rules for sound combinations (e.g., English forbids [tl] at syllable onset, so fatlump is segmented as fat lump; Bulgarian allows [tl], so Bulgarian infants do not use [tl] as a boundary cue). 3. Sound Production: From Approximation to Mastery # Perception-Production Gap: Children understand words they cannot pronounce (e.g., clock → [gak], desk → [deks])—their phonological representations (perception) are adult-like, but articulatory skills (production) are not. Typical Production Errors: Follow predictable patterns to simplify articulation: Substitution: clock → [gak] (voiceless /k/ → voiced /g/). Metathesis: desk → [deks] (sound reordering: /dɛsk/ → /dɛks/). Consonant Harmony: dog → [gog] (initial consonant matches final one). 2.2 Section 5.2: Learning Word Meanings # Explores the efficiency of L1 vocabulary growth and the cognitive tools that resolve meaning ambiguity.
1. Vocabulary Growth: Timeline & Efficiency # Developmental Milestones: 12 months: 1st words (object labels/social terms: Daddy, juice). 18–20 months: 50 words (slow growth, as children test meaning hypotheses). 20+ months: “Great vocabulary spurt” (1–2 new words/day). Ages 2–6: 10 words/day (add abstract terms: happy, yesterday). Proficiency Benchmarks: Age 6 = 14,000 words; High school = 60,000 words (including academic vocabulary). Key Observation: L1 learning is far more efficient than L2 (2-year-olds learn 70+ words/week; adults learn 5–10 L2 words/week). 2. The Gavagai Problem & Cognitive Assumptions # Key Problem (Quine 1960): When hearing gavagai while seeing a rabbit, children cannot logically know if it means “rabbit,” “furry,” or “running”—they use 4 innate assumptions to narrow meaning: Whole Object Assumption (Markman & Hutchison 1984): New words label entire objects (e.g., gavagai = whole rabbit, not its paw). Type Assumption (Clark 1993): New words label categories (e.g., dog = all dogs, not just “Fido”). Basic Level Assumption (Hall & Waxman 1993): New words refer to mid-level categories (e.g., dog instead of superordinate mammal or subordinate golden retriever). Mutual Exclusivity Assumption (Markman & Wachtel 1988): No two words have identical meanings (e.g., if a child knows spoon, they infer fendle refers to an unfamiliar whisk). 3. Verb Meaning Acquisition: Challenges & Syntactic Bootstrapping # Why Verbs Are Harder: They require linking abstract actions to thematic roles (e.g., eat needs an Agent = eater, Theme = food) and depend on context. Syntactic Bootstrapping (Gleitman 1990): Children use a verb’s syntactic frame to infer meaning (e.g., Mary clessed the toy car to her baby brother → frame = Noun-Verb-Noun-to-Noun → meaning = “transfer” (like give)). Verb Overgeneralization: Normal developmental step (e.g., Don’t giggle me—extending intransitive giggle to transitive frame; I’m singing him—extending sing to “sing to him”). 2.3 Section 5.3: Acquisition of Functional Morphology and Syntax # Focuses on how children learn grammatical rules (functional morphology) and sentence structure (syntax).
1. Functional Morphology: Rules, Errors, and Developmental Order # Functional vs. Lexical Morphology: Functional morphemes (e.g., -ing, -s plural) are grammatical “engine” components; lexical morphemes (e.g., mommy, run) carry meaning. Rule Learning: The Wug Test (Berko Gleason 1958): Design: 4–5 year-olds saw a “wug” (novel creature); when shown two, they were asked “Now there are two __?” Finding: 75% produced wugs (plural) and wugged (past tense)—proving children learn general rules, not just memorize words. U-Shaped Development (Past Tense): Stage 1 (Early): Correct irregulars (went, ate) (memorized). Stage 2 (Middle): Overgeneralization (goed, eated) (applying -ed rule to all verbs). Stage 3 (Late): Correct regulars (walked) and irregulars (went) (restricting rules to regular verbs). Brown’s 14 Grammatical Morphemes (Brown 1973): Universal acquisition order (tied to complexity and phonetic salience): Progressive -ing (19–28 months) Prepositions in/on (27–33 months) Regular plural -s (27–33 months) Irregular past (25–46 months) Regular past -ed (26–48 months) 3SG -s (28–50 months) 2. Syntax Acquisition: Stages, MLU, and Complex Structures # Developmental Stages: One-Word Stage (12–18 months): Single words stand for full propositions (e.g., cow = “Look at the cow”). Two-Word Stage (18–24 months): Follows native word order (e.g., English SVO: Mommy fix, give doggie)—reflects emerging thematic role knowledge (Agent, Theme). Multiple-Word Stage (24+ months): Longer utterances with functional morphemes (e.g., I’m gonna sit on her) and complex structures (relative clauses, questions). MLU (Mean Length of Utterance): Measures syntactic growth (total morphemes in 100 utterances ÷ 100). Example: Eve (20 months) = MLU 1.7 (mommy go); Eve (28 months) = MLU 3.5 (mommy is driving the car). Complex Structures: Wh-Question Asymmetry: Subject Questions (e.g., Who is helping Mary?): Simple (no auxiliary movement over subject)—high accuracy. Object Questions (e.g., Who is Mary helping?): Complex (wh-word moves from object to start, crossing more syntactic nodes)—low accuracy (children simplify: What did he play? instead of What did he play with?). 2.4 Section 5.4: Acquisition of Semantics and Pragmatics # Explores the acquisition of abstract meaning (semantics) and context-dependent communication (pragmatics), both delayed due to computational complexity.
1. Semantic Acquisition: Viewpoint Aspect # Viewpoint Aspect: Encodes how speakers “view” an event (imperfective = ongoing; perfective = completed). Cross-Linguistic Errors: Example 1 (Italian): 3–5 year-olds accept completed events for imperfect tense (e.g., Marta mangiava una mela = “Marta was eating an apple” → accept “Marta ate the whole apple”); adults reject this. Example 2 (Russian): 3–6 year-olds guess randomly at imperfective verbs without temporal context; with context (While he was writing, the phone rang), accuracy jumps to 80%. Why Aspect Is Hard: Requires linking morphology to abstract event properties (not concrete objects) and integrating discourse context (mastered by age 6+). 2. Pragmatic Acquisition: Scalar Implicatures # Scalar Implicatures: Inferences where a weaker term (e.g., some) implies negation of a stronger term (e.g., not all). Study Example (Papafragou & Musolino 2003): Design: All 5 horses jump; puppet says “Some of the horses jumped.” Findings: Adults (92.5%) reject the description (some = not all); 5-year-olds (12.5%) accept it (interpret some literally = “at least one”). Why Implicatures Are Hard: Children default to literal meaning—they lack perspective-taking skills to ask “Why didn’t the puppet say all?” Improvement Strategies: Explicit scales (some vs. all) or context highlighting speaker intent boost 6-year-olds’ accuracy to 70%. 3. Unifying Constraint: Computational Complexity # Key Claim: Semantic/pragmatic delays stem from needing to compare multiple meaning options and integrate context—taxing working memory. Semantics (Aspect): Compare “incomplete” vs. “completed” event views. Pragmatics (Implicatures): Compare literal (some = at least one) vs. pragmatic (some = not all) meanings and infer speaker intent. Developmental Timeline: Improves with working memory/cognitive maturity (ages 6–8). 2.5 Section 5.5: Bilingual First Language Acquisition # Resolves the “one system vs. two systems” debate and explains cross-linguistic influence in 2L1 learners.
1. Evidence for Two Differentiated Grammatical Systems # Early Language Separation: 8–12 month-old bilinguals show language-specific sensitivity (e.g., distinguish L1/L2 prosody; use L1 with L1-only caregivers, L2 with L2-only caregivers—no code-switching in monolingual interactions). Matching Monolingual Stages (Genesee 1989, Meisel 1989): French-English/German-French bilinguals reach the two-word stage (18–24 months) and acquire morphology (e.g., English -ing, French -ant) at the same age as monolinguals. Monolingual-Like Errors: Spanish-English bilinguals make Spanish null-subject errors (Hablas español = “Speak Spanish”)—same as monolingual Spanish children; no mixed errors (Speak español). 2. Cross-Linguistic Influence: Constraints and Examples # Influence occurs in specific domains, not randomly:
Domain 1: Syntax-Discourse Interface: Example (Pronoun Reference): English-Italian bilinguals make 30% more errors in Italian (interpreting null pronoun ø as referring to the daughter, not mother)—English’s ambiguous pronouns “bleed” into Italian. Example (Null-Subject Transfer): Spanish-English bilinguals use 25% more overt subjects in Spanish (Tú hablas español) than monolinguals—transferring English’s requirement for overt subjects. Domain 2: Processing Economy: Example (Dutch-French Wh-Questions): French allows wh-in-situ (Tu fais quoi? = “What are you doing?”); Dutch requires wh-movement (Wat doe je?). Bilinguals produce 40% wh-in-situ errors in Dutch (Jij doe wat?)—transferring French’s simpler structure to reduce processing load. 3. Factors Shaping Cross-Linguistic Influence # Three key determinants:
1. Input Quantity (Language Dominance): Influence flows from dominant (more exposure) to non-dominant language. Example: L2-dominant (80% English) German-English bilinguals make 60% German gender errors (die Hund instead of der Hund)—transferring English’s lack of grammatical gender. 2. Structural Ambiguity: Influence occurs when one language has ambiguous structures. Example: Spanish’s Hablas español (ambiguous: “You speak” vs. “Speak”)—bilinguals interpret it as imperative 35% more often than monolinguals (reinforced by English’s single imperative analysis of Speak Spanish). 3. Processing Demands: Bilinguals avoid complex structures. Example: Dutch’s wh-movement is more complex than French’s in-situ—bilinguals transfer French’s structure to Dutch. 3. Post-Learning Consolidation # 3.1 Chapter Takeaways # L1 acquisition follows universal stages but uses language-specific cues (e.g., English trochaic stress vs. Spanish prosody). Cognitive assumptions (whole object, mutual exclusivity) drive efficient L1 vocabulary learning. Functional morphology and syntax develop via rule-learning (not memorization), with U-shaped patterns for irregulars. Semantics/pragmatics are delayed due to computational complexity—mastered by ages 6–8. Bilingual first language learners develop two separate grammars, with cross-linguistic influence shaped by input, ambiguity, and processing demands. 3.2 After-Class Tasks # Mini Reflection (150–200 words):
Choose one L1 domain (sound, vocabulary, grammar) and explain how a child’s cognitive development supports learning (e.g., how working memory affects aspect acquisition). Self-Check Questions: What is the “Perception-Production Gap” in L1 sound acquisition? Why do children overgeneralize past tense rules (e.g., goed)? What evidence proves bilingual first language learners have two separate grammars? How does input quantity shape cross-linguistic influence?

title: Ch.7: ACQUISITION OF (FUNCTIONAL) MORPHOLOGY
content:
Chapter 7 — ACQUISITION OF (FUNCTIONAL) MORPHOLOGY # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 7: Acquisition of (Functional) Morphology. Link to Chapter 7
1. Pre-Class Preview Guide # 1.1 Chapter Core Focus # This chapter explores how learners acquire functional morphology (grammatical morphemes like -ing, past tense -ed, 3SG -s) in second language (L2) acquisition. It addresses key questions: Do L2 learners follow fixed acquisition orders? Why do they struggle with morphology even if their syntax is intact? And what theories explain these challenges?
1.2 Key Learning Objectives # By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Describe the fixed order of L2 functional morphology acquisition and how it relates to L1 patterns. Distinguish between “syntax-before-morphology” and “morphology-before-syntax” views. Compare major hypotheses (RDH, MSIH, PTH, FRH) explaining L2 morphology challenges. Analyze learner data to identify syntax-morphology dissociation and prosodic transfer effects. Explain how universal features are “reassembled” for L2 functional morphology. 1.3 Preview Questions (To Guide Reading) # Why do early L2 studies (e.g., Dulay & Burt) argue for a fixed morpheme order? What evidence supports the “syntax-before-morphology” view (e.g., Patty’s case)? How do RDH and MSIH differ in explaining L2 morphology errors? What is “prosodic transfer,” and how does it affect L2 morphology production? What does the Feature Reassembly Hypothesis (FRH) mean by “reassembling universal features”? Preview & Scaffolding # 1. Why This Preview Matters # Chapter 7 ties 3 areas together:
Morphology: Small word parts (e.g., -ed, -s). Syntax: Sentence structure (e.g., subject-verb order). Meaning: What you want to convey (e.g., past time). This preview clarifies the basics so theories make sense later.
2. Key Morphology Types # Chapter 7 focuses on inflectional morphology (grammar markers)—not derivational (word-creators).
Type What It Does Examples Derivational Makes new words/word classes teach → teacher, happy → unhappiness Inflectional (focus) Adds grammar info (no new word) walk → walks, cat → cats 3. Functional vs. Lexical Morphemes # Functional morphemes = grammar glue (no standalone meaning); lexical = content words (carry ideas).
Type Function Examples What It Adds Lexical Conveys concepts (objects/actions) dog, run, beautiful “What” is happening/being Functional Signals grammar relationships -ed, -s, the, if “When”/“how”/“which one” Example # She walked the dog: Lexical: walked (action), dog (object). Functional: -ed (past time), the (specific dog). 4. Core Functional Morpheme Categories # These are the “grammar tools” Chapter 7 discusses—each links to a syntax “slot” (e.g., Tense Phrase).
Category Example Job Syntax Link Tense/Aspect -ed, -ing Marks when an event happens Tense Phrase (TP) Agreement -s (3SG) Makes subject/verb “match” (e.g., he walks) Agreement Phrase (AgrP) Determiners a, the Marks if a noun is specific Determiner Phrase (DP) Complementizers that, if Links clauses (e.g., I think that she left) Complementizer Phrase (CP) 5. Syntax–Morphology–Meaning: How They Work Together # Grammar is a 3-layer system—learners often master the first two before the third.
Layer What It Does Example Step L2 Common Error 1. Meaning Convey your idea (e.g., past action) “I ate lunch earlier.” None—idea is clear. 2. Syntax Organize words (correct order) I eat lunch earlier Word order is right. 3. Morphology Add grammar markers (surface form) I ate lunch earlier I eat lunch earlier (missing -ed). → Errors usually happen at Layer 3 (morphology)—not meaning/syntax.
6. Functional Categories (Syntax “Slots”) # These are invisible “slots” in sentences that functional morphemes fill (e.g., TP = tense slot).
Category What It Does Example Sentence Link T (Tense) Marks time (past/present) She walks (present) Agr (Agreement) Makes subject/verb match He likes (3SG subject → -s) D (Determiner) Marks specific/non-specific The cat (specific cat) 7. The Big Chapter 7 Question # Chapter 7 debates: Does syntax (structure) come before morphology (form)?
View Core Claim Example Prediction Syntax-before-morphology Structure first, form later He walk = knows TP (needs subject/tense) but misses -s. Morphology-before-syntax Form first, structure later He walk = no TP yet (no tense/agreement slot). Chapter 7 mostly supports syntax-before-morphology (e.g., Patty uses overt subjects but omits -s).
8. Key Term Cheat Sheet # Term Simple Definition Interpretable Feature Adds meaning (e.g., [past] = “before now”) Uninterpretable Feature Grammar-only (e.g., -s = subject-verb match) Mapping Linking abstract grammar to surface form 9. Chapter 7 Roadmap # You’ll learn 4 theories to explain L2 morphology errors:
RDH: Missing grammar “slots” (e.g., no agreement). MSIH: Intact slots, but can’t retrieve the form (e.g., forget -ed). PTH: L1 rhythm affects form (e.g., stressing THE). FRH: Need to “rearrange” grammar features (e.g., L1 vs. L2 tense markers). Use this preview to link each theory to the basics above!
3. Core Content (By Section) # Each section includes Key Takeaways, Core Concepts & Evidence, and Key Study Examples to simplify preview and review.
Section 7.1: Morpheme Studies # Key Takeaways # L2 functional morphology has a (mostly) fixed acquisition order, but early studies overlooked L1 transfer and overuse errors—revised methods (e.g., Stauble’s accuracy) give a more realistic view of “mastery.”
Core Concepts & Evidence # Foundational L1 Precedent: Brown’s (1973) Functor Order
Brown tracked 3 English L1 children and found 14 functional morphemes (e.g., -ing, plural -s) are acquired in a fixed order:
Progressive -ing (19–28 months) → prepositions in/on (27–33 months) → plural -s (27–33 months) → 3SG -s (28–50 months). Order depends on complexity (fewer grammatical features = earlier) and phonetic salience (easier to perceive = earlier). L2 Morpheme Order: Creative Construction Hypothesis
Dulay & Burt (1973, 1974): Spanish/Chinese L1 children learning English showed the same accuracy order (high for -ing/plural -s, low for possessive ’s/3SG -s)—even with different L1s, proving innate grammar (not just L1 transfer) guides acquisition. Bailey et al. (1974): Adults follow the same order as children (e.g., -ing early, 3SG -s late)—fixed order is a general L2 pattern. Criticisms & Method Improvements
Early flaws: Ignored L1 transfer (e.g., Spanish L1 learners master plural -s faster than Japanese L1 learners, as Spanish has plural morphology) and overuse errors (e.g., using -ing for imperatives like Sitting down!). Stauble’s (1984) revised accuracy: Includes overuse in calculations (denominator = obligatory contexts + overused contexts) to avoid overestimating mastery. “Acquired” Cutoff Debates
No universal standard—each reflects a theory:
90% correct (Brown): Measures “full adult-like mastery.” 60% correct: Signals “emerging grammar” (above chance). First productive use: Marks when a structure enters the learner’s grammar. Key Study Example # Dulay & Burt (1973) BSM Task: 5–8-year-old Spanish L1 children with varying English exposure (Sacramento = high, East Harlem = low) all showed congruent accuracy: 85% for -ing, 30% for possessive ’s—proving fixed order. Section 7.2: Syntax-before-morphology # Key Takeaways # L2 learners acquire the syntax of functional categories (e.g., obligatory subjects, tense meaning) first—morphology gaps reflect surface mapping issues, not broken syntax.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Competing Views
Morphology-before-syntax: Learners need surface morphology (e.g., 3SG -s) to “activate” syntax (e.g., TP structure) (Vainikka & Young-Scholten). Syntax-before-morphology (White 2003): Learners master syntactic properties (e.g., overt subjects) first; morphology lags due to mapping challenges (not lack of syntax). Empirical Evidence for Syntax-Morphology Dissociation
Lardiere’s (1998a,b) Patty Case: Mandarin L1 adult L2 English learner with 4.5% accuracy for 3SG -s and 34.5% for past -ed—but 98% overt subjects and 100% nominative case. Her intact syntax proves she has a functional TP; low morphology is a surface issue. Li’s (2012) Child Learners: Mandarin L1 children L2 English show 16% accuracy for 3SG -s but 100% overt subjects—same dissociation as adults. Semantic Support
Slabakova (2003): Bulgarian L1 learners (no L1 tense-aspect morphology) mastered English aspect meanings (e.g., progressive = ongoing) despite poor morphology—proving semantic/syntactic knowledge comes first. Key Study Example # Patty’s TP Performance: She correctly uses overt subjects (He takes the bus, not Takes the bus) and nominative case (he vs. him) but omits 3SG -s (He take). This shows her TP syntax is intact—morphology is the only gap. Section 7.3: Representational Deficit Hypothesis (RDH) # Key Takeaways # RDH argues L2 morphology errors reflect deep syntactic deficits (missing/unvalued features), not just surface issues—but it fails to explain partial accuracy and syntax-morphology dissociation.
Core Concepts & Evidence # RDH Core Claim
Adult L2 learners cannot fully acquire abstract morphosyntactic features absent in their L1. Morphology errors (e.g., missing past -ed) mean the associated syntactic category (e.g., TP) is impaired.
RDH Variants
Variant Core Claim Valueless Features Hypothesis (Eubank) L2 features (e.g., agreement) are “inert” and can’t trigger syntax. Failed Functional Features Hypothesis (Hawkins & Chan) Learners can’t reset L1 parameters (e.g., null subjects). Interpretability Hypothesis (Hawkins et al.) Only meaning-linked features (e.g., noun gender) are acquirable—syntax-only features (e.g., adjective gender concord) are not. Supporting Evidence
Hawkins & Liszka (2003): Chinese L1 learners (no L1 tense morphology) have 63% past -ed accuracy, while German/Japanese L1 learners (with L1 tense) have 92%—RDH attributes this to impaired TP in Chinese learners. Franceschina (2001, 2005): English L1 L2 Spanish learner Martin has 95% accuracy for noun gender (meaning-linked) but 60% for gender concord (syntax-only)—aligns with Interpretability Hypothesis. Limitations
Can’t explain partial accuracy (e.g., 63% past -ed—if TP is impaired, accuracy should be random). Ignores syntax-morphology dissociation (e.g., Patty’s intact TP syntax). Key Study Example # Martin’s Gender Performance: He correctly assigns gender to nouns (el perro = “the dog”) but struggles with adjective concord (el perro negra instead of negro). RDH argues this is because noun gender is meaning-linked (acquirable), while concord is syntax-only (unacquirable). Section 7.4: The Missing Surface Inflection Hypothesis (MSIH) # Key Takeaways # MSIH rejects representational deficits—L2 learners have intact syntax but struggle to map abstract features to surface morphology (e.g., retrieving -s for [3SG] features).
Core Concepts & Evidence # MSIH Core Claim
Morphology is “missing on the surface, not in the syntax.” Learners know syntactic features (e.g., [3SG, present]) but fail to retrieve the corresponding morphology (e.g., -s) during production.
Empirical Evidence
Haznedar & Schwartz (1997) Erdem Case: Turkish L1 L2 English child (4–5 years) uses 90% overt subjects (syntactic finiteness) but 85% uninflected verbs—proves he understands finiteness; morphology retrieval is the issue. Prévost & White (2000a,b) Adult Learners: L2 French/German learners use infinitives in finite positions (e.g., je manger instead of je mange) but avoid finite verbs in non-finite positions—shows they know finiteness rules; they just default to easier-to-retrieve infinitives. Mechanism: Distributed Morphology
Syntax is built first (with features like [3SG]); lexical items (e.g., -s) are inserted late. L2 learners may insert default forms (e.g., infinitive take) if the target (e.g., takes) is inaccessible.
Teaching Relevance
Focus on automatic retrieval: Drill high-frequency inflections (e.g., 3SG -s) in context to reduce retrieval load.
Key Study Example # Erdem’s Development: Early on, he says I play (overt subject = good syntax) but not I playED (missing morphology). Later, his morphology accuracy rises to 60%—proving retrieval improves with practice, not syntax. Section 7.5: The Prosodic Transfer Hypothesis (PTH) # Key Takeaways # PTH adds that L2 morphology gaps come from L1 prosodic transfer—learners apply L1 rules for stress/word structure to L2, misaligning with L2’s prosodic requirements.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Prosodic Structure Basics
Phonology is hierarchical: Segments → Syllables → Feet → Prosodic Words (PWd) → Phonological Phrases. Languages differ in how they attach morphology to these levels (e.g., English -ed is “adjoined” to PWd; Mandarin aspect markers are “integrated” in PWd).
Supporting Evidence
Goad & White (2008) Articles: Mandarin/Turkish L1 L2 English learners stress articles (THE book, A mat)—transferring L1 prosody (Mandarin has no unstressed words; Turkish stresses definite markers). Goad & White (2006) Past Tense: Mandarin L1 learners produce -ed with non-native strong release (e.g., /t/ for played)—transferring Mandarin’s prosodic prominence rules. PTH vs. MSIH
They complement each other: MSIH explains retrieval gaps; PTH explains position/phonetic errors (e.g., omitting articles after disyllabic verbs like catches [the] mat).
Key Study Example # Mandarin L1 Article Stress: Learners say THE cat (stressed the) because Mandarin has no unstressed function words—this is prosodic transfer, not lack of article knowledge (they use the correctly in strong positions). Section 7.6: The Feature Reassembly Hypothesis (FRH) # Key Takeaways # FRH argues L2 morphology acquisition is about reassembling universal features (not learning new ones)—learners adapt L1 feature bundles to L2’s category/form-meaning mappings.
Core Concepts & Evidence # FRH Fundamentals
All languages use universal features (e.g., [past], [gender]). L2 learners:
Identify which features L2 uses. Map features to L2’s lexical category (e.g., [past] on verbs in English, complementizers in Irish). Learn L2’s form-meaning links (e.g., -ed = [past] + [perfective]). Form-Meaning Mismatches: English -ed
Lardiere (2005, 2007) shows -ed encodes 4 meanings (e.g., [+past] = We devoured; politeness = I was wondering). Learners acquire them incrementally (core first, then secondary).
Cross-Linguistic Category Mismatches
Language [past] Feature Host Form L2 Challenge English Verb -ed Mandarin L1: Map [past] to verbs. Irish Complementizer gurL English L1: Map [past] to complementizers. Supporting Evidence: Shimanskaya (2015)
English L1 L2 French learners:
Beginners transfer L1 [Human] (he/she = [+Human], it = [–Human]) to French clitics (le/la = no [Human]), making gender errors for inanimates. Advanced learners drop [Human] and use French’s [gender]-only system (99% accuracy)—proving reassembly. Key Study Example # French Clitic Reassembly: Advanced learners correctly use la for both [+Human] (la fille) and [–Human] (la table)—they reassembled from L1’s [Human]+[gender] to L2’s [gender]-only bundle. 3. Post-Class Review Tools # 3.1 Chapter Takeaways Summary # L2 functional morphology has a fixed order, but L1 transfer and overuse errors modify it. Syntax develops before morphology—low morphology accuracy ≠ broken syntax. RDH (deficits) vs. MSIH (retrieval) vs. PTH (prosody) vs. FRH (reassembly): Together, they explain most L2 morphology gaps. Reassembly of universal features is key for advanced L2 morphology mastery. 3.2 Self-Check Questions # Why did Dulay & Burt’s cross-linguistic study (Spanish/Chinese L1) support the Creative Construction Hypothesis? How does Patty’s case (Lardiere) contradict the Morphology-before-syntax view? What’s the difference between RDH and MSIH in explaining 3SG -s errors? Give an example of prosodic transfer affecting L2 morphology. What does FRH mean by “reassembling” features (use English → Irish [past] as an example)? 3.3 Quick Reference: Hypothesis Comparison # Hypothesis Core Explanation for Morphology Gaps Key Strength Key Weakness RDH Impaired syntactic features (absent in L1) Explains L1 transfer effects Ignores syntax-morphology dissociation MSIH Surface retrieval of morphology Aligns with syntax-before-morphology evidence Doesn’t explain prosodic errors PTH L1 prosodic transfer Explains position/phonetic errors Focuses only on production FRH Reassembling universal features Accounts for cross-linguistic variability Needs more data on beginner reassembly

title: Ch.8: ACQUISITION OF SYNTAX
content:
Chapter 8 — ACQUISITION OF SYNTAX # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 8: Acquisition of Syntax. Link to Chapter 8
1. Pre-Class Preview Guide # 1.1 Chapter Core Focus # This chapter explores the acquisition of syntax (sentence structure and grammatical dependencies) in second language (L2) learning, with a focus on three core themes: how the concept of “syntactic parameters” has evolved, whether L2 learners develop native-like syntactic representations, and how cross-linguistic differences (e.g., word order, verb movement, wh-movement) shape acquisition.
1.2 Key Learning Objectives # By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Trace the historical evolution of the “parameter” concept—from early “binary switches” to modern feature-based models. Distinguish between Representational Deficit and Full Functional Representation accounts of L2 syntax acquisition. Analyze how L2 learners acquire cross-linguistic word order differences (e.g., SVO vs. SOV) and verb movement patterns (e.g., French vs. English). Explain universal constraints on wh-movement (island constraints) and their role in testing Universal Grammar (UG) access in L2. Interpret empirical data to evaluate which theoretical frameworks best explain L2 syntax acquisition. 1.3 Preview Questions (To Guide Reading) # Why did early “parameter switch” models fail to explain L2 syntax acquisition? What evidence supports the claim that L2 learners can develop native-like syntactic representations (Full Functional Representation)? How do L1 transfer and UG interact in L2 word order acquisition (e.g., Greek SVO → Turkish SOV)? Why do French L1 learners of English struggle with question formation even after mastering adverb placement? What are “island constraints,” and how do they prove UG access in L2 wh-movement acquisition? 2. Core Content Review (By Section) # Each section includes Key Takeaways, Core Concepts & Evidence, and Key Study Examples—aligned with the source document’s modular structure for easy preview/review.
Section 8.1: A Historical Excursion into the Notion of Parameter # Key Takeaways # The concept of “syntactic parameters” (language-specific variation) has evolved from “binary switches” (triggering clusters of constructions) to lexically encoded feature bundles (per the Minimalist Program). Early models failed empirically, while modern frameworks focus on incremental feature reassembly.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Early Parameter Model (1980s–1990s): Binary Switches & Clusters
Core Idea: Parameters are on/off switches paired with universal principles (e.g., Subjacency). A single switch setting triggers a “cluster” of related constructions (like a light switch controlling multiple lights). Flagship Example: Null Subject Parameter (NSP) (Rizzi 1982): Spanish (NSP = On): Allows null subjects (Mangia come una bestia = “He/she eats like a beast”), null expletives (Piove oggi = “It rains today”), and postverbal subjects (Ha telefonato uno studente = “A student called”). English (NSP = Off): Prohibits these constructions (e.g., *Eats like a beast is ungrammatical). Empirical Failures of Early Models
L2 NSP Studies (White 1985, Hilles 1986): Spanish L1 learners of English mastered postverbal subjects but still produced null subjects—contradicting the “cluster” prediction (if one NSP construction is mastered, all should be). Verb Movement Parameter (White 1990): Francophone L2 English learners mastered adverb placement (e.g., John often kisses Mary) but failed at question formation (e.g., *Likes she John?), proving no cluster acquisition. Modern Reconceptualization (2000s–Present): Feature-Based Parameters
Core Idea: Parameters are not switches but universal feature bundles on lexical items (e.g., verbs, complementizers). Languages differ in which features they select and which lexical category hosts them. Example: Tense feature [past] is universal but encoded on: Verbs (English: walked). Complementizers (Irish: gurL thuig sé = “that-Past understood he”). Nouns (Somali: árdday-gii = “student-Det.Masc.Past” = “former student”). Current Thinking: Cognitive Primitives & Sentence Domains
Ramchand & Svenonius (2014) propose a cross-linguistically fixed sentence hierarchy linked to cognition: Verb Domain (V): Encodes the action/state (e.g., Mary eat a sandwich). Tense Domain (T): Anchors the event in time (e.g., Mary ate a sandwich). Complementizer Domain (C): Links the sentence to discourse (e.g., Did Mary eat a sandwich?). Key Study Example # White (1985) NSP Study: Spanish L1 learners of English accepted null subjects 40% of the time (vs. 80% accuracy for French L1 learners) but mastered postverbal subjects—proving NSP does not act as a single switch. Section 8.2: Representational Deficit vs. Full Functional Representation # Key Takeaways # Two frameworks debate L2 syntactic representations: Representational Deficit argues L2 learners have permanent gaps (uninterpretable features absent in L1 cannot be acquired), while Full Functional Representation claims learners develop native-like representations (errors stem from surface performance, not defective syntax).
Core Concepts & Evidence # Representational Deficit Accounts
Core Claim: Adult L2 learners lack access to some universal features—uninterpretable features (regulate syntax, e.g., adjective gender concord) absent in L1 are permanently unacquirable. Key Variants: Fundamental Difference Hypothesis (Bley-Vroman): Learners rely on domain-general strategies (not UG) and L1 transfer—native-like syntax is impossible. Interpretability Hypothesis (Hawkins et al.): Only meaning-linked (interpretable) features (e.g., noun gender) are acquirable; syntax-only features are not. Example (Tsimpli & Dimitrakopoulou 2007): Greek L1 learners of English still accepted ungrammatical resumptive pronouns (*Who do you think that Susan would marry him?) at advanced stages—claimed as proof of permanent deficit. Full Functional Representation Accounts
Core Claim: L2 learners have intact syntactic representations—errors come from surface issues (e.g., feature mapping, lexical retrieval), not defective syntax. Key Variants: Full Transfer Full Access (FTFA, Schwartz & Sprouse): Learners transfer L1 features initially but retain UG access to reset parameters. Missing Surface Inflection Hypothesis (MSIH, Prévost & White): Syntax is intact; morphology gaps reflect mapping challenges (e.g., Patty’s 4.5% 3SG -s accuracy but 98% overt subject accuracy, Lardiere 1998a,b). Example (Leal Méndez & Slabakova 2014): Advanced French L1 learners of English rejected ungrammatical [Human] pronoun errors (*It is Mary) at 92% accuracy—matching natives (96%), proving no permanent deficit. Empirical Test Cases
Test Case Representational Deficit Prediction Full Functional Prediction Outcome (Supports) English [Human] pronoun feature (French L1) Cannot acquire [Human]—accept *It is Mary Acquire [Human]—reject *It is Mary Full Functional Wh-island constraints (Chinese L1) Cannot acquire Subjacency—accept *Who did you wonder whether… Acquire Subjacency—reject ungrammatical sentences Full Functional Key Study Example # Patty’s Case (Lardiere 1998a,b): Mandarin L1 L2 English learner with 4.5% 3SG -s accuracy but 98% overt subject accuracy—proves TP (Tense Phrase) syntax is intact; only surface morphology is missing (supports MSIH). Section 8.3: Word Order # Key Takeaways # L2 word order acquisition starts with L1 transfer but progresses to L2 norms via UG. Canonical orders (e.g., Turkish SOV) are acquired early, while non-canonical orders (e.g., Turkish OSV) require integrating multiple features (word order + case + specificity)—slowing progress.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Cross-Linguistic Word Order: Prevalence & Cognitive Roots
Typological Dominance: SVO (~35.4%, e.g., English) and SOV (~45%, e.g., Turkish) dominate because they align with human cognition (Agent → Action → Patient). Rare Orders: VSO (e.g., Irish) and OSV are rare—L2 acquisition is slower due to cognitive dissonance. Theoretical Evolution of Word Order
1980s: VP Headedness Parameter: SVO = head-initial VP (verb before object); SOV = head-final VP (verb after object). 1990s (Kayne 1994): Universal SVO: All languages have underlying SVO—SOV results from object movement to pre-verbal position. 2000s+: Lexical Diacritics: Verbs carry diacritics (e.g., English eat = [+pre-object]; Turkish yemek = [+post-object])—L2 learners acquire these to produce correct order. L2 Word Order Acquisition: Transfer & UG
Early Transfer (FTFA): Greek L1 (SVO) learners of Turkish (SOV) initially produce SVO (Mary yedi bir elma = “Mary ate an apple”) but shift to SOV (Mary bir elma yedi) with input (Papadopoulou et al. 2011). Feature Interaction Challenge: Non-canonical orders (e.g., Turkish OSV: Bir elma Mary yedi = “An apple Mary ate”) require integrating word order, Accusative case (-i), and specificity—intermediate learners have 49% case accuracy (vs. 95% verbal inflection), limiting OSV mastery. Key Study Example # Papadopoulou et al. (2011) Greek-Turkish Study: Beginners mastered Turkish SOV (canonical order) but failed at OSV (non-canonical, needs case + specificity). Advanced learners improved OSV accuracy to 72%—proving incremental feature integration. Section 8.4: Verb Movement # Key Takeaways # Verb movement (verbs moving to Tense/Complementizer vs. staying in Verb Phrase) is not a parametric switch—L2 acquisition involves incremental feature mapping. The Verb-Second (V2) rule (German) is acquired late due to rare input but mastered by advanced learners.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Cross-Linguistic Verb Movement: French vs. English
French: Verbs move to Tense (T)/Complementizer (C)—supports verb-adverb (S-V-Adv-O: Jean embrasse souvent Marie), verb-negation (S-V-Neg-O: Marie n’aime pas Jean), and question inversion (V-S-O: Aime-t-elle Jean?). English: Verbs stay in Verb Phrase (VP)—requires adverb before verb (S-Adv-V-O: John often kisses Mary), do-support for negation/questions (S-Aux-Neg-V-O: Mary does not like John). Early Verb Movement Parameter: Failed Cluster Predictions
White (1990) Francophone L2 English Study: Learners taught adverb placement showed no improvement in question formation—proving no cluster acquisition (undermines “switch” model). Verb-Second (V2) Rule: German Case Study
V2 Rule: Finite verbs must be the second constituent in German main clauses (e.g., Im Park hat er sie gefunden = “In the park had he her found”). L2 Acquisition: Beginners: 49.3% V2 violations (e.g., *Im Park er hat sie gefunden = “In the park he had her found”). Advanced: 100% accuracy (Conradie 2006)—explained by Yang’s Variational Learning Model (rare unambiguous V2 input: 1.2% of child-directed speech) and Multiple Grammars Hypothesis (coexisting L1/L2 subgrammars). Key Study Example # Conradie (2006) Afrikaans V2 Study: South African English L1 learners of Afrikaans (V2 language) showed 100% V2 accuracy at advanced stages—proving UG access to complex verb movement. Section 8.5: Wh-movement # Key Takeaways # Wh-movement (wh-phrases moving to clause start) is constrained by universal “island rules” (prohibiting movement out of certain structures). L2 learners acquire these constraints via UG—proving Full Functional Representation, even if L1 lacks wh-movement.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Cross-Linguistic Wh-movement: In-situ vs. Movement
Wh-movement Languages (English): Wh-phrases move to CP (e.g., What did John buy?; *John bought what? is ungrammatical for regular questions). Wh-in-situ Languages (Mandarin): Wh-phrases stay in base position (e.g., Hufei mai-le shenme? = “Hufei bought what?”). Island Constraints: Universal Limits
Island types (prohibit wh-movement out of bounded structures): Wh-islands: *Who did you wonder whether this girl danced with? Complex NP islands: *Who did you spread a rumor that this girl danced with? Poverty of the Stimulus: Learners never hear ungrammatical island sentences—acquiring constraints proves UG access. L2 Wh-movement: Evidence for UG
Martohardjono (1993): Chinese/Indonesian L1 learners of English rejected strong island violations (87%/76% accuracy) more than weak ones—mirroring natives (99%/78% accuracy), proving UG access. Li (1998): Chinese L1 learners in China (classroom input) and Canada (naturalistic input) had comparable island constraint accuracy—input type does not block UG use. Key Study Example # Johnson & Newport (1991) Chinese L1 Study: Adult Chinese L1 learners of English reliably distinguished grammatical (non-island) and ungrammatical (island) wh-movement—accuracy above chance, proving Subjacency acquisition via UG. 3. Post-Class Review Tools # 3.1 Chapter Takeaways Summary # Parameters evolved from “switches” to feature bundles—L2 acquisition involves incremental feature reassembly, not holistic switch-setting. Full Functional Representation better explains L2 syntax: Learners develop native-like representations; errors are surface issues (not deficits). Word order/verb movement acquisition starts with L1 transfer but progresses via UG—complexity rises with feature interaction. Wh-movement island constraints are acquired via UG—proof of innate syntactic principles in L2. 3.2 Self-Check Questions # Why did early parameter models (e.g., NSP cluster) fail to explain L2 syntax acquisition? How does Patty’s case (Lardiere 1998a,b) support Full Functional Representation? What makes Turkish OSV (non-canonical word order) harder to acquire than SOV (canonical)? Why is German V2 acquired late by L2 learners (per Yang’s model)? How do island constraints prove UG access in L2 wh-movement acquisition? 3.3 Quick Reference: Framework Comparison # Framework Core Claim About L2 Syntax Key Strength Key Weakness Representational Deficit Permanent gaps (uninterpretable features unacquirable) Explains L1 transfer effects Ignores native-like advanced performance Full Functional Representation Native-like representations (errors = surface issues) Aligns with UG access evidence Needs more data on beginner feature reassembly

title: Ch.9: ACQUISITION OF THE MENTAL LEXICON
content:
Chapter 9 — ACQUISITION OF THE MENTAL LEXICON # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 9: Acquisition of the Mental Lexicon. Link to Chapter 9
1. Pre-Class Preview Guide # 1.1 Chapter Core Focus # This chapter explores how the mental lexicon (the brain’s storage system for words) works in bilinguals, covering key topics like how L1/L2 words are stored and retrieved, how bilinguals inhibit one language to speak another, how complex words are decomposed, and how learners acquire word meaning extensions (e.g., metonymy).
1.2 Key Learning Objectives # By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Distinguish between the Revised Hierarchical Model (RHM) and BIA+ Model of bilingual lexicon representation. Explain how bilinguals inhibit non-target languages (Green’s Inhibitory Control Model) and the cognitive effects of this inhibition. Analyze how L2 learners decompose polymorphemic words (e.g., worked = work + -ed) using Ullman’s Declarative/Procedural Model. Identify challenges in acquiring verb argument structure (e.g., causative-inchoative alternations) when L1 and L2 differ. Interpret transfer of reference (metonymy) in L2 and explain why regular metonyms are easier to acquire than novel ones. 1.3 Preview Questions (To Guide Reading) # How do beginner vs. advanced bilinguals differ in linking L2 words to concepts (e.g., cat → “cat”)? Why do bilinguals take longer to switch from L2 back to L1 (e.g., Spanish → English → Spanish)? Do L2 learners store worked as a whole word or decompose it into work + -ed? How does proficiency affect this? What errors do Chinese L1 learners of English make with psychological verbs (e.g., disappoint)? Why do advanced L2 learners understand read Dickens (regular metonymy) but struggle with read Needham (novel metonymy)? 2. Core Content Review (By Section) # Each section includes Key Takeaways, Core Concepts & Evidence, and Key Study Examples—aligned with the source document’s modular structure for easy preview/review.
Section 9.1: Mental Representation and Access of Lexical Items # Key Takeaways # Bilinguals’ mental lexicon is integrated (L1 and L2 words stored together), not separate. Lexical access is language-nonspecific (both languages activate at once), and two models explain representation: RHM (mediated L2-concept links for beginners) and BIA+ (feature-based activation across L1/L2).
Core Concepts & Evidence # Foundational Terms: Lexeme vs. Lemma
Lexeme: Stores formal properties (spelling, pronunciation) — e.g., cat /kæt/, cats /kæts/. Lemma: Stores semantic (meaning) and syntactic (word class) properties — e.g., cat = [+noun, +animate, “small feline”]. L1 children acquire lemmas first; lexemes develop with repeated exposure. Bilingual Lexicon Models
Model Core Claims Key Example Revised Hierarchical Model (RHM, Kroll & Stewart 1984) - Separate L1/L2 lexical stores; shared conceptual store. - Beginners: L2 → L1 → Concept (e.g., cat → gato → “cat”). - Advanced: Direct L2 → Concept links. Spanish L1 learners of English: Early reliance on gato to understand cat; advanced learners link cat directly to “cat.” BIA+ Model - Three levels: Feature (letters/sounds), Lexical (L1/L2 words), Conceptual (lemmas). - Activation spreads across levels (no “language nodes”); context selects the target word. Seeing blue activates English blue, Dutch blut (“pale”), and blus (“blouse”) — context (English reading) selects blue. Empirical Evidence for Integrated Lexicon
Cross-Linguistic Activation: Spanish-English bilinguals hearing “Pass the cup” look at a spoon (Spanish cuchara, starts with /k/) — proves L2 activation (Marian & Spivey 2003). Homograph Effect: Dutch-English bilinguals slow down when reading ramp (English = “slope”; Dutch = “disaster”) — interference from L2 meaning (van Heuven et al. 2008). Neuroimaging: High-proficiency Chinese-English bilinguals activate the same brain areas (left frontal/temporal) for L1 and L2 — no separate “language regions” (Chee et al. 1999). Factors Influencing Lexical Access
Proficiency: Low L2 proficiency → more brain activation (compensatory processing); high proficiency → native-like activation. Frequency: High-frequency words (e.g., the) are accessed faster; “personal frequency” (how often a learner uses a word) matters more than corpus frequency. Key Study Example # Chee et al. (2001) Proficiency Study: Low-proficiency Chinese L2 English learners activate the right inferior frontal gyrus (compensation); advanced learners activate only left hemisphere areas (same as L1) — proves proficiency shapes access efficiency. Section 9.2: Inhibition of One Language to Speak Another # Key Takeaways # Bilinguals use inhibition to suppress non-target languages (Green’s Model). Inhibiting the dominant L1 (to speak L2) is more effortful, causing “switch costs” — but constant inhibition strengthens executive function (bilingual cognitive advantage).
Core Concepts & Evidence # Green’s Inhibitory Control Model (1998)
Core Problem: Parallel language activation (e.g., cuchara activates when speaking English spoon) requires inhibition to avoid mixing. Language Task Schema: A top-down mechanism that: Identifies the target language (e.g., English) via context. Inhibits non-target language activation (e.g., Spanish). Selects the target word (e.g., spoon). Dominance Effect: Inhibiting L1 (dominant) for L2 production requires more effort than inhibiting L2 for L1. Empirical Proof of Inhibition
Switch Costs (Meuter & Allport 1999): Dutch-English bilinguals naming numerals show larger delays when switching L2→L1 (+90ms) than L1→L2 (+50ms) — L1 inhibition “spills over” to slow L1 access. ERP N2 Component: Switch trials (e.g., L1→L2) show 20% larger N2 amplitudes (neural marker of inhibition) than non-switch trials — confirms active inhibition (Abutalebi 2008). Voluntary Switching (Gollan & Ferreira 2009): Even when choosing to switch, bilinguals have higher RT costs for L2→L1 — L1 inhibition is persistent. Bilingual Cognitive Advantage
Constant inhibition strengthens executive function: Stroop Test: Bilinguals name ink color (e.g., “red” in blue) 15% faster than monolinguals. Task Switching: Bilingual children switch between sorting tasks 20% faster. Neural Basis: More efficient anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) — the brain’s “conflict resolver” (Abutalebi et al. 2012). Key Study Example # Meuter & Allport (1999) Numeral Naming: Japanese-English bilinguals (Japanese-dominant) show L2→L1 switch costs of +85ms (vs. L1→L2 +45ms) — proves dominant L1 requires stronger inhibition, supporting Green’s Model. Section 9.3: Morphological Decomposition in the Lexicon # Key Takeaways # L2 learners decompose polymorphemic words (e.g., worked) differently than natives: Beginners store words as wholes (declarative memory), while advanced learners decompose regular inflections (procedural memory). Morphologically rich languages (e.g., Russian) force earlier decomposition.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Ullman’s Declarative/Procedural Model
Two memory systems drive morphological processing:
Memory System Function Role in Morphology Example Declarative Stores arbitrary info (vocab, facts). Whole-word storage (irregular/rare words). kept (stored as a whole, not keep + -t). Procedural Applies rules to combine units. Decomposition (regular/frequent words). worked = work + -ed (via past tense rule). L1 vs. L2: Adults rely more on declarative memory for L2 morphology (procedural memory weakens with age). Testing Decomposition
Lexical Decision Task: If decomposed, stem frequency (not whole-word frequency) drives RT — natives show no frequency effect for regulars (e.g., worked vs. scribbled); L2 learners do (store whole words). Masked Priming: A masked stem (e.g., work) speeds RT for worked if decomposed — natives show priming; beginners do not (Neubauer & Clahsen 2009). L2 Decomposition Patterns
Beginners: Store all polymorphemic words as wholes (e.g., gearbeitet [“worked” in German] = whole word, not arbeit + -t). Advanced: Decompose regular inflections (e.g., -ed, -s) but struggle with derivations (e.g., bitterness from bitter). Morphologically Rich Languages: Russian learners decompose inflections (e.g., rabotaju = rabotaj + -u) early — too many forms to store whole (Gor & Jackson 2013). Key Study Example # Neubauer & Clahsen (2009) German Participles: German natives show no frequency effect for regulars (decomposed) but a frequency effect for irregulars (stored whole). Polish L2 learners show a frequency effect for both — proves they store all participles as wholes (declarative memory). Section 9.4: Argument Structure # Key Takeaways # Argument structure (verb meaning → required arguments, e.g., break needs Agent + Theme) is challenging for L2 learners due to cross-linguistic mismatches. Overt morphology (e.g., Spanish se for inchoatives) and universal semantic primitives (e.g., CAUSE, BECOME) help acquisition.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Key Alternations
Causative-Inchoative Alternation: Causative: John broke the vase (Agent + Theme). Inchoative: The vase broke (Theme only). Cross-Linguistic Marking: Spanish uses se (El barco se hundió = “The ship sank”); English has no marking — Spanish L1 learners master the alternation faster. Dative Alternation: Double-object: Mary sent John the package (entails possession). Dative: Mary sent the package to John (no possession). L2 Error: Overgeneralization to verbs like push (*Sam pushed Molly the package) — ignores possession constraints. Cross-Linguistic Mismatches: Psychological Verbs
English conflates CAUSE + STATE in one verb: The book disappointed Mary (Theme = book, Experiencer = Mary). Chinese requires a periphrastic structure: Nei ben shu rang Zhang San shiwang = “That book made Zhang San disappointed.” Juffs (1996): Advanced Chinese L1 learners accept The book disappointed Mary at 85% accuracy — prove they acquire L2 conflation via universal primitives. Unaccusativity: Universal Split
Unergatives: Agent subject (e.g., John danced — allows cognate objects: John danced a jig). Unaccusatives: Theme subject (e.g., The vase broke — no cognate objects: *The vase broke a break). L2 Challenge: German uses auxiliaries (sein for unaccusatives, haben for unergatives) — English L1 learners struggle to match auxiliaries to verb type. Key Study Example # Montrul (2000) Causative-Inchoative Study: L2 Spanish learners (L1 English) use se in inchoatives at 90% accuracy by intermediate level (vs. 65% for English L2 learners of Spanish) — overt morphology provides clear argument structure cues. Section 9.5: Transfer of Reference # Key Takeaways # Transfer of reference (metonymy) is extending a word’s referent (e.g., ham sandwich = “customer”). L2 learners master regular metonyms (lexicalized, e.g., Bordeaux = “wine”) faster than novel metonyms (context-dependent, e.g., seat 19 = “passenger”) due to cultural gaps and processing load.
Core Concepts & Evidence # What Is Metonymy?
Conceptual mapping between related entities (e.g., object→person: ham sandwich = customer; place→event: Vietnam = “Vietnam War”). Distinction from Metaphor: Metonymy = association (The White House = U.S. government); metaphor = similarity (He is a lion = brave). Regular vs. Novel Metonymy
Type Traits Example Regular Lexicalized (dictionary-listed), no context needed. Read Dickens = “read books by Dickens”; Bordeaux = “wine from Bordeaux.” Novel Context-dependent, requires inference. Read Needham = “read books by Needham”; seat 19 = “passenger in seat 19.” L2 Acquisition Challenges
Cultural Gaps: The White House issued a statement — learners without U.S. context misinterpret “White House” as a building. Processing Load: Novel metonyms require extra inference — Dutch-English bilinguals take 510ms to process read Needham (vs. 380ms for read Dickens, Frisson & Pickering 2007). L1 Transfer: Spanish learners overuse “place for event” metonyms (mirroring Spanish) but adapt with proficiency (Slabakova et al. 2014). Key Study Example # Frisson & Pickering (2007) Eye-Tracking: Advanced Dutch-English bilinguals have 98% accuracy for regular metonyms (read Dickens) but 72% for novel ones (read Needham) — proves context and lexicalization drive comprehension. 3. Post-Class Review Tools # 3.1 Chapter Takeaways Summary # Bilingual lexicon is integrated — L1/L2 words activate together; access depends on proficiency and context. Inhibiting dominant L1 causes switch costs but strengthens executive function (bilingual advantage). L2 morphological decomposition shifts from whole-word (beginners) to rule-based (advanced) — driven by memory systems. Argument structure acquisition relies on universal semantic primitives and overt morphology. Regular metonyms are easier to acquire than novel ones — cultural knowledge and lexicalization matter. 3.2 Self-Check Questions # How do RHM and BIA+ differ in explaining L2→concept links for beginners? Why do L2→L1 switch costs (e.g., Spanish→English→Spanish) exceed L1→L2 costs? What memory system do beginners use for worked? What about advanced learners? Why do Chinese L1 learners of English initially avoid The book disappointed Mary? What makes Bordeaux (regular metonym) easier for L2 learners than seat 19 (novel metonym)? 3.3 Quick Reference: Key Phenomena & Explanations # Phenomenon Key Explanation Cross-linguistic activation (e.g., cuchara activates for spoon) Integrated lexicon (BIA+ Model) — no separate language nodes. Larger L2→L1 switch costs Green’s Model — inhibiting dominant L1 requires more effort. L2 decomposition of gearbeitet (German) Ullman’s Model — beginners use declarative memory (whole-word); advanced use procedural (decomposition). Chinese learners’ disappoint errors Cross-linguistic conflation mismatch — Chinese lacks CAUSE+STATE verbs. Novel metonymy struggle High processing load — requires context inference (no lexicalization).
